outcome: Help payment providers select the best compliant route for each cross-border payment to improve delivery speed, transparency, success rate, and risk-adjusted margin.
overview: Cross-border payments pass through several correspondents, FX providers, compliance checks and settlement windows, yet route selection is usually static: customers get little price or timing transparency while the provider absorbs failure, repair, liquidity and FX cost. This solution scores every eligible route on fee, FX rate, expected delivery time, liquidity, counterparty performance, compliance status and historical success, predicts repair or rejection risk before submission, and explains the route it chose within treasury policy. Sanctions, anti-money-laundering and limit controls remain authoritative gates ahead of scoring. An eight to twelve week historical proof of value evaluates selected corridors before any controlled routing, targeting more successful payments, faster delivery and better risk-adjusted margin.

benefits.text: Improve straight-through payment success by a target 5–10% in the selected corridors
benefits.limits: Basis: hypothesis. Target range to validate on the customer’s own corridor history against a control group — not a guarantee

benefits.text: Reduce repair, rejection and investigation cost by a target 15–30%
benefits.limits: Basis: hypothesis. Depends on the quality of repair-reason coding in the customer’s current operations data

benefits.text: Improve risk-adjusted contribution per payment by pricing fee, FX and liquidity cost into the routing decision
benefits.limits: Basis: hypothesis. Requires authoritative fee and FX feeds and a finance-agreed transaction-level cost ledger

benefits.text: Give customers a pre-payment fee, FX and delivery-time estimate, and give operations an explained route decision
benefits.source: Reference design — pre-payment quotation and decision logging, Redington BFSI catalogue
benefits.limits: Estimate accuracy is bounded by correspondent data quality and by settlement-window behaviour outside the provider’s control

residency: Deployable in-country on local AWS or Azure regions (e.g. UAE, KSA); payment message, route and counterparty data remain within the customer tenancy, with corridor-by-corridor review of any cross-border data movement

notFor.situation: Only one viable route exists in the corridors of interest
notFor.why: Optimisation needs alternatives to choose between; a single correspondent leaves nothing to score

notFor.situation: End-to-end fees, FX rates and message status cannot be linked back to an individual transaction
notFor.why: Route economics and success prediction are both transaction-level; aggregate reporting cannot attribute either

notFor.situation: Sanctions and anti-money-laundering screening cannot be placed ahead of route scoring
notFor.why: Compliance eligibility is a gate, not a score; a route that fails screening must never enter the ranking

notFor.situation: No manual fallback exists if the routing service is unavailable
notFor.why: Payment finality and settlement deadlines make an unavailable optimiser an operational incident, not an inconvenience

scope:
Model: Joint delivery: accredited implementation partner leads, with Redington architecture and commercial governance; the customer retains payment, compliance, treasury and correspondent accountability throughout · Duration: 8–12 weeks to historical proof of value; a further 18–32 weeks to production depending on hub and correspondent integration
Delivery pod: Partner project lead + payments technical lead, vendor platform specialist, data scientist; customer payments sponsor, operations lead, treasury and FX manager, MLRO and compliance reviewer, data owner, security and architecture reviewers, finance analyst and correspondent relationship owner · Support model: 24×7 production option with severity-based response targets; partner service desk with vendor escalation and a defined correspondent escalation path; optional managed corridor optimisation
1) Discovery and corridor baseline agreement
2) Corridor, route and control-group design
3) Payment and route data preparation
4) Historical route simulation and model validation
5) Treasury and compliance policy configuration
6) Payment-hub, screening and treasury integration
7) Security, resilience and performance testing
8) UAT and operations training
9) Controlled routing launch
10) Stabilisation and handover

Route explanations and audit records complete; operations and treasury users trained
